name: GnuTLS
listed_description: Secure communication library, implementing SSL, TLS and (description truncated in the lead)
reason: No numeric comparison in GnuTLS's favour reachable. Read the full 434 KB NEWS file (3.8.13 back to 2000) and the manual chapters cha-gtls-app, cha-internals, cha-library, cha-intro-tls plus README from gitlab.com: the only performance items are internal (3.6.0 lock-free per-thread random generator with no numbers; 3.6.5 side-channel-silent RSA decryption making RSA handshakes 13% to 28% slower than GnuTLS's own earlier code; faster CA import and faster library init, no numbers). Web searches found no GnuTLS-versus-OpenSSL win: snippets show only historical talk of GnuTLS being 30% to 50% slower, a 2009 gnutls-help thread saying mod_gnutls was faster than mod_ssl in some configurations (lists.gnupg.org EGRESS_BLOCKED, no numbers seen), gnutls-cli benchmark output for GnuTLS alone, and OpenSSL asm borrowed into GnuTLS. Directional at best. The guessed category concurrency-queues-locks is wrong (a TLS library, wave 5 tls).

name: happly
listed_description: A C++ header-only parser for the PLY file format. Parse .ply happily!
reason: No performance claim in README or repo (README and github.com page checked: features only, no benchmark, no comparison). The guessed baselines printf and snprintf are wrong: happly is a PLY mesh parser. The only third-party numbers found point the other way: a PLY parser benchmark (ton/PLYbench, seen through a search snippet only) reports hapPLY 18.79x slower overall than the fastest parser, 28.90x slower on ASCII, 12.31x on binary big endian and 15.15x on binary little endian, slower than tinyply (8.97x) and RPly (11.24x). Slower than its peers, so no faster-than-baseline record.

name: Hashmaps
listed_description: Implementation of open addressing hash table algorithms in C++.
reason: No numeric comparison against a named external baseline reachable. README is two sentences; main.cc and the Makefile only run its five own variants (linear probing, Robin Hood with tombstones, Robin Hood with backward shift deletion, hopscotch bitmap and shadow) through loading, batch and ripple tests that measure when insertion fails and verify integrity, with no timings and no std::unordered_map. The author's blog posts that use this code (codecapsule.com Robin Hood hashing backward shift deletion, hopscotch hashing) are EGRESS_BLOCKED; a search snippet says they compare the variants by probe-distance metrics (DIB, DMB in bytes), not time against std::unordered_map. The 2-3x std::unordered_map snippet (4698 ms vs 1473 ms) seen in web search was not tied to goossaert's repo.

name: heman
listed_description: Tiny library of image utilities dealing with height maps, normal maps, distance fields and the like
reason: No numeric comparison anywhere reachable. README (calls itself a toy project), docs/overview.rst, docs/index.rst and include/heman.h contain no timings, benchmark or baseline; the repo has src, include, test and docs but no benchmark directory. Only directional pointers to 'fast' published algorithms (Felzenszwalb distance transform, Bridson Poisson disk sampling, Sean Barrett's ambient occlusion sweeps) and an OpenMP build note. The guessed baseline 'standard image codec' is wrong: heman is a heightmap and normal-map utility, not a codec.
